Analysis by Richard Cowan

Things are not going well in the Afghan war, but for the most part it has been“off-topic”

, so I have only had a couple of posting son the subject, until now.

From2002,see

Afghan Opium Crop Booms Under DEAland Control As Feds Focus On Cannabis,

Reverse Policy On Prosecuting Small Medical Growers In Washington State; Cut 6

Plants In California; Seize Bongs In Illinois.

andfrom2004,see

Remembrance and Ignorance: In Afghan fields the poppies grow...

By 2002 it was already obvious that there was a fundamental conflict between the

objectives of the war against the Taliban and the so-called“war on drugs.”If the US and

its NATO allies tried to destroy the Afghan opium crop, we would alienate the poorest

peasants for whom it was a badly needed cash-crop, as well as some of our war lordallies,

for whom it was a source of wealth and power.

On the other hand, if we just ignored it, the Taliban would be able to get significant funding

from it. Naturally, we chose to do both. We would oscillate between attacking the crop sand

ignoringthem.Thatwaywewouldmaximizetheprofitsandpoliticalopportunitiesforthe

Taliban, plus increase prices for heroin in Europe, where most of the Afghan opium/heroin

endedup.

In a further ironic twist, we left much of the poppy producing area to the Canadians, under

a brain-dead Tory government that is more prohibitionist than even GeorgeBush.

On the other hand, our Dutch allies are not happy with their part of the mess. On April 20th

(yes,4/20) of this year, Radio Netherlands carried a story quoting“a Dutch officer who

fumes that the Netherlands is again following the US and its"stupid"war on drugs."It's

undermining our whole mission and it's certainly undermining my motivation."

Dutch areas in Uruzgan province were said to be"relatively safe",and Dutch soldiers are

“welcome guests”after spending millions of euros on reconstruction projects.

However, when the Afghan forces begin destroying poppy fields, the Dutch were required

to give them back-up. A Dutch soldier is quoted as saying: "This is only going to make our

work much harder. Just last week I was in a village shouting through a megaphone:

'Don't worry, we won't destroy your poppy fields.'"

Cannabis to the rescue?

Finally, just this month, the US prohibitionists finally gave in to their allies. Thomas

Schweich, principal deputy assistant secretary for the Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs (what a title!) conceded, "We have decided to stop pursuing

the aerial spraying of poppy fields in Afghanistan."

But it gets even better. The very prohibitionist London Times (owned by Rupert Murdoch)

carried a story on the 8th of this month:“CANNABIS IS THE NEW DRUG OF CHOICE

FOR AFGHANISTAN'S FORMER OPIUM POPPY FARMS”

It began so romantically,“Where opium poppies used to colour the plains of northern

Afghanistan, towering cannabis plants now sway in the wind, filling the air with their pungent

odour.”

Then quite prosaically, it explains,“Farmers in Balkh province were banned from cultivating

opium last year and have switched to another cash crop, a rich source of income that is still

tolerated by the authorities...

Excerpt:

Growing cannabis is nothing new for Afghan farmers, but the opium clampdown has

transformed a minor cash crop into big business. The 2007 annual report of the UN Office on

Drugs and Crime estimated a 40 per cent rise in Afghanistan's cannabis production this year

from 50,000 hectares ( 123,550 acres ) last year to 70,000 hectares this year.

The switch from opium to cannabis is the latest embarrassment to Western attempts at

eradication. It also illustrates the desperation of poor farmers.”…

Unlike opium, cannabis is smoked by some farmers without serious social consequences.

"The only thing is there seem to be more layabouts now that we grow so much cannabis." one

said….

Some Western officials try to look on the bright side. One said: "At least they've gone from

producing hard drugs to soft drugs. It's progress, sort of."

However, one should not put too much trust in the common sense of the prohibitionists.

Meanwhile, back in Great Bonkers, The Telegraph (now also very prohibitionist) reports,

“At a time when the military is desperately short of men, more than 1,500 troops—the

equivalent of two battalions—have failed drug tests in the past two years, with a 60 percent

increase in drug abuse since 2003.”

Stress is seen as a major cause of the problem, and cocaine use has more than quadrupled

since 2003, overtaking cannabis for the first time. Cocaine now accounts for around 50% of

all positive drug tests, up from 22%. Cannabis accounts for only 30% of failures.

The Telegraph article cites Prof. Sheila Bird, who is a senior scientist with the Medical

Research Council; however, it did not report everything she said.

A similar article in The Guardian, which is the last major anti-prohibitionist paper in the

UK, also reports,“Bird suggested soldiers' drug use may have shifted away from cannabispartly to minimise their chance of testing positive. Traces of cocaine disappear from urine

quicker than cannabis.”

In other words, the UK may be losing the greater part of a battalion a year because of

cannabis prohibition, even as the allies cheer the fact that Afghan farmers are switching to

cannabis.

If people weren’t dying, this would be a farce, but it is just one more tragedy.

So,Ishouldexplainthatthequoteinthetitle,“Words are, of course, the most powerful drug

used by mankind”isfromRudyardKipling,andweshouldalsolethimhavethelastword:

“When you're wounded and left on Afghanistan's plains, and the women come out to cut up

what remains, jest roll to your rifle and blow out your brains and go to your gawd like a

soldier.

”
